summary.summary: Westmorland and Furness closed 2025/26 with a quiet treasury position: no new external borrowing was taken, the council instead covering previously approved borrowing need from short-term cash reserves rather than paying for new loans. Debt stood at £173.6m (average rate 3.7%) against £74.6m of temporary investments (average 4.07%) at 31 March 2026, and treasury management came in £6.3m under its £14.65m budget thanks to high interest earned on retained cash balances. The report confirms all treasury activity complied with the prudential indicators and the February 2025 strategy. Full Council was also asked to approve a revised 2025-2031 capital programme of £591.1m at outturn, up from £432.1m when first set in February 2025, with outturn slippage of £10.1m and accelerated spend of £12.6m.

compliance.notes: A strong core TMSS: five-year prudential indicator suite, a 13-year four-balance liability benchmark, a CDS-informed creditworthiness policy and a well-reasoned borrowing strategy. Weakest areas are commercial/non-treasury disclosure (proportionality recited but never quantified, no PI-08 ratio, no IMPs, no exit/fair-value substance) and formal governance hooks (no four-clause adoption statement, scrutiny committee unnamed); indicator tables omit prior-year actuals throughout, and the capital strategy in force dates from June 2024 with the 2026/27 refresh still in draft at TMSS time. Scored from the council-website final versions because the moderngov packet URLs (s40871/s37305) sit behind a Cloudflare challenge.

news_drafts.headline: Westmorland and Furness reserves of £41.6m projected to run out by 2028-29 or 2030-31, auditor says
news_drafts.lead:
Westmorland and Furness Council's external auditor has projected that the council's revenue reserves, which stood at £41.6m at the end of 2025-26, would be used up without exceptional financial support. That is permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The auditor's annual report goes to the Audit Committee on 25 November and carries a key recommendation on the council's finances.

The £41.6m is made up of a £14.9m general fund balance and £26.7m of earmarked reserves. The report gives two dates for depletion. Its executive summary says the reserves would be completely depleted by 2030-31, while its financial sustainability section says by 2028-29.

The auditor describes the council's financial position as high-risk. The council has a savings target of £30.9m for 2026-27. The report says: "Should planned savings fail to materialise, or alternative funding sources not be secured, the Council may need to seek exceptional financial support (EFS) from central government to maintain financial sustainability."

news_drafts.headline: Westmorland and Furness plans for £5.2m a year of schools deficits from 2028/29 when override ends
news_drafts.lead:
Westmorland and Furness Council's revised five-year financial plan assumes it will have to meet £5.172m a year of schools-funding deficits from 2028/29, when a temporary government protection is expected to end. The plan goes to the council's Cabinet on 13 October.

The protection is the statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) off their main balance sheet. The plan assumes it ends on 31 March 2028. From 2028/29 the council expects to carry 10% of the yearly deficit on high needs (the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities), which it puts at £2.548m. It also expects to carry all of the yearly schools deficit, put at £2.624m.

The paper, the 2026-2031 Revised Medium Term Financial Plan (the council's financial plan for the coming years, showing the gap between expected spending and income), says the assumption "is not a definitive position". It states: "the MTFP forecast reflect the current statutory position with further information awaited from government." The figures are therefore built on the rules as they stand now, and the council has not yet had government's decision on what follows the override.
news_drafts.paper_title: CAB 13/10 - 2026-2031 Revised Medium Term Financial Plan

news_drafts.headline: Westmorland and Furness capital forecast shows £4.818m slippage on high needs school provision
news_drafts.lead:
Westmorland and Furness Council's first-quarter forecast for 2026/27, put to the full council on 24 September, shows £4.818m of slippage on its high needs school provision. It is the largest deferral of any single scheme in the council's capital programme. The capital programme is the council's planned spending on things that last, such as buildings, roads and equipment. High needs is the part of school funding that supports children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The scheme had a forecast of £2.876m for the year. After the slippage, the 2026/27 budget for it is £1.0m. Slippage means spending planned for one year is now expected to fall later.

The appendix to the report sets out the figures scheme by scheme, and the high needs line is the biggest movement among them. The material available does not give the reason for the deferral.

findings.headline: Council consulting on discretionary home-to-school transport spending as part of budget setting
findings.detail: The auditor cites Cabinet's approval to consult on discretionary expenditure areas, with papers setting out cost implications, anticipated savings, and the split between statutory and discretionary provision.
findings.matters: A council moving discretionary transport spending into a formal consultation as part of savings is a choice other councils facing the same pressure will compare.
findings.quote: consultation on discretionary areas of expenditure relating to home-to-school transport

findings.headline: Council may need exceptional financial support if planned savings fail or alternative funding is not secured
findings.detail: The auditor says the council's financial position is high-risk. If savings are not delivered, the council may need to seek exceptional financial support from central government to stay financially sustainable.
findings.matters: Exceptional financial support would change the council's funding and borrowing position, and is the outcome lenders and peer councils would most want to anticipate.
findings.figures: £30.9m savings target 2026-27; EFS referenced as a possible outcome
findings.quote: Should planned savings fail to materialise, or alternative funding sources not be secured, the Council may need to seek exceptional financial support (EFS) from central government to maintain financial sustainability.

findings.headline: 2026-27 budget balanced using £30.9m of savings, £3m of reserves and £3m of provisions
findings.detail: The budget depends on three sources to balance. The savings target is 10.2% of the net budget requirement, against 3.2% delivered in previous years, according to the paper.
findings.matters: A balanced budget that draws on reserves and provisions, with a savings target three times the historic rate, is the structure a lender or peer finance team will want to see stress-tested.
findings.figures: £30.9m savings; £3m reserves; £3m provisions released; savings target 10.2% of net budget requirement; 3.2% in previous years
findings.quote: The 2026-27 budget is balanced but requires delivery of £30.9m of savings, the use of £3m of reserves and release of £3m of provisions.

findings.headline: Significant weakness in procurement and contract management arrangements maintained, with progress from prior year
findings.detail: The auditor has raised a key recommendation on procurement and contract management and an improvement recommendation. Progress is noted from the prior year, and the council is implementing a new procurement system.
findings.matters: A continuing weakness in contract management is a control risk any council with a large contract base would want to track.
findings.figures: One significant weakness; one key recommendation; one improvement recommendation
findings.quote: A significant weakness in arrangements is maintained in relation to procurement and contract management arrangements, although progress noted from prior year.

findings.headline: Governance value-for-money rating moves from red in 2024-25 to amber in 2025-26
findings.detail: The auditor reports no significant weaknesses in governance arrangements this year, and four improvement recommendations. The paper credits improvements in decision making, risk management and internal audit.
findings.matters: A change in the auditor's rating for governance shows how the council's arrangements have moved after a previous significant weakness.
findings.figures: Governance rating: red (2024-25) to amber (2025-26); four improvement recommendations
findings.quote: moving the Council from a red -rating in 2024-25 to an amber-rating in 2025-26
